reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Wyatt waited at the bus stop with Grandpa. The sun was bright and warm. Wyatt wore his sunny hat. Then the wind blew. It blew the hat right off! Wyatt laughed. "Come back, hat!" The wind pushed a leaf, too. Wind pushed the hat, and the hat pushed the leaf. What a silly wind!

Then dark clouds came. Rain began to fall. Grandpa opened the umbrella. Plip, plip, plop. Then Wyatt heard something. Rumble! It was thunder, loud and sharp. Wyatt wanted to stay and splash in the rainy puddles. But Grandpa took his hand. "Thunder says go indoors," said Grandpa. So they hurried home, fast, fast, fast.

Inside, they looked out the window. The rain fell and fell. Wyatt zipped up his cozy jacket. "Thunder told us to come in," said Wyatt. Grandpa smiled. "Yes it did."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Sarah was at Grandma's house. Grandma poured milk into ten little cups on the table. "How many cups, Grandma?" asked Sarah. "Let's count them," said Grandma.

Sarah started at the red cup. "One, two, three, four, five." Grandma started at the blue cup at the other end. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six." They both pointed at cups, one by one, slowly.

"You got ten too?" said Sarah. "I got ten from my side!" She counted again from the middle cup. Ten cups again. She counted from the cat's side. Ten cups again. The gray cat sat under the table and washed his dirty paw.

"Now for the cookies," said Grandma. She put three cookies on one plate and six on another plate. "Which plate has more?" Sarah pointed at each cookie. "This one! This one has more." Grandma smiled and gave her the big plate. "One, two, three, four, five, six," said Sarah.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Brielle got to school early. Her teacher put a pencil on her table.

"Today we write your name," said Miss Kim. Brielle was so happy. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

Brielle picked up the pencil. She jumped up to show her friend Leo. The pencil point waved up in the air. Leo leaned in close to look. The point came near his eye. Miss Kim rushed over fast.

Brielle stopped. She looked at her pencil. She turned it around. Now the point faced down. She walked to Leo slowly, holding it that way. The point stayed far from his face.

"See my pencil?" said Brielle. "Point down."

"Nice holding," said Leo.

Brielle sat back down. She gripped the pencil near the tip. She made a big round B. Then two little r's. She wrote her whole name, one letter at a time.

"I did it!" she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "You counted seven letters," she said.

"Is that a joke?" asked Brielle. "My name is not that long!"

Brielle wrote her name again. It looked even better the second time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Charlotte went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about dogs. Dogs had four legs and floppy ears.

She found a big picture book. On one page she saw a cow. On the next page she saw a fish. The fish had no legs at all.

"That fish is silly," said Charlotte. "It is not an animal. Animals have legs." She looked at the dog page. She looked at the cow page. Then she looked at the fish again.

Charlotte turned the wheel on the book rack. Round and round it went. All the animal books spun by. Dogs, cows, birds, and fish too.

"Fish live in the water," said Charlotte softly. "But they are still animals." She wanted to yell the good news. Instead she ran to her dad.

"Dad! Fish are animals!" she said.

"That's right," said Dad. "Want to check out that book?"

"Yes, please," said Charlotte. She hugged the big book. Then she picked one more, all about toy trucks and apples and bread.

At home she read the fish page twice.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair bounced as she looked around. On the wall there was a picture of a dog with a bandage on its arm.

"Today you get a shot," said Mom.

Mila frowned. She thought a shot would be very big. She imagined a needle as tall as the door. She imagined it would hurt for a long, long time. She held her bear tight.

"I don't want a big poke," said Mila.

The doctor came in. She held up a small needle. It was thin, like a little stick. It was not tall like the door at all.

"You can hug your bear," said the doctor. "Just look at him."

Mila hugged her bear. She looked at his soft ear. The doctor touched Mila's arm.

"One quick poke," said the doctor.

Mila felt a tiny pinch in her arm. Then it was done. The doctor put on a round bandage. It had yellow stars on it.

"That's it?" asked Mila.

"That's it," said the doctor. "All done."

Mila looked at her arm. The poke was already over. She had waited for something big. But it was just quick and small.

Mila showed Mom her star bandage. "It was fast," she said. "My bear got one too."

The doctor put a small bandage on the bear's arm. Mila smiled and walked out slowly, holding her bear up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Lennon held Mom's hand at the store. Yesterday they had no bread. Today the bread shelf was full.

"Is today the library day?" Lennon asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day. It is happening right now."

Lennon picked a small bread loaf. It felt soft, like a little mouse. She put it in the cart. She wanted to read her library book now.

"We go to the library later," Mom said. "First we pay now."

A man next to them had weak hands. His apples fell and rolled. Lennon picked up one apple. She held it out to him.

"Here," she whispered.

"Thank you, little one," he said.

They paid for the bread. Then Mom smiled.

"Now we go to the library. Today is the day."

Lennon skipped all the way to the car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ayla waited in a little room at the doctor's office. She wanted her sticker, but first the doctor had to check her. "Can you see my light?" the doctor asked. Ayla looked with her eyes. She saw the small light blink on and off.

Then the doctor held up a bell. Ding, ding! Ayla heard it with her ears. She sniffed with her nose when the doctor opened a mint tin. It smelled cool and sweet. The doctor gave her a tiny taste on a stick. It tasted like orange.

"Now one more check," the doctor said. She took off Ayla's shoes and socks. She set Ayla's bare feet on a soft green mat. "It feels like grass," the doctor said. Ayla wiggled her toes. The soft grass tickled her feet. She laughed out loud. "Grass feet!" said Ayla. The doctor laughed too, and gave her the sticker.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mateo ran into Grandma's house. He wanted to hold the new baby. Baby Rosa was sleeping in a little basket.

"I want to hold her now," said Mateo.

"Not standing up," said Grandma. "Come sit with me."

Mateo sat down on the soft couch. Grandma sat right beside him. Then she put Rosa in his arms. "See? You can hold her while you sit," she said.

Rosa was small and warm. She made a tiny sound. Her hand opened and closed. Mateo laughed. "She is trying to tickle me!"

Then Rosa spit up a little. It was slimy on Mateo's shirt. "Yuck!" he said. Grandma wiped it with a cloth. "Babies do that," she said, and she smiled.

Grandpa brought Mateo a glass of milk. Mateo drank it all up. He could not move with the baby, so Grandpa held it for him.

Rosa blinked her eyes. Then she fell asleep in Mateo's arms. He sat very, very still.

"Shh," said Mateo. "My baby is sleeping."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim suit all by herself. "Today I will swim," she said.

The pool was big and blue. A lifeguard sat in a tall chair. "Why does she sit up so high?" Leah asked her mom. "I want to see." Leah walked to the side of the pool. From the floor, she could see her mom's knees. Then she sat on the wide step. Now she could see more. Then she stood on the step and looked. From up high, she could see every swimmer in the pool. "I see the whole pool!" she said. The lifeguard was looking at everyone too.

Leah saw a small boy splashing near the rope. The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed to him. A grown-up swam over and helped him. "She saw him from up high," said Leah. The pool was quiet again. Leah jumped a little jump into the water. The lifeguard smiled down at her from the tall chair. "I can see you!" Leah called up.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Hudson threw the beanbag high over his shoulder. It flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a thumping sound. Miss Kim picked it up. She smiled. "Watch me," she said. She held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped right into the hoop.

"Can I try that?" Hudson asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. Hudson held the beanbag low. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag rose in the air. It landed on the edge of the hoop. "So close!" said his friend Milo.

Hudson tried again. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up and fell into the hoop. "I did it!" Hudson said. Milo clapped his hands.

Next Miss Kim rolled a big blue ball to Hudson. He caught it with both hands. He laughed. "That throw was a little messy," Milo said, pointing at his own shoes. Hudson had stepped in a puddle from the rain. "That's okay," Hudson said. He threw the beanbag again. It landed in the hoop one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Asher ran to the playground. He wanted the red swing. But a big girl was on it. Asher's face got hot. He stomped his foot. "I want a turn!" he shouted.

His dad knelt down next to him. "Let's try something," Dad said. "Breathe in slow. Now breathe out slow." Asher made a big breath in. He let it out like a sleepy dragon. Again, in and out. His hot feeling got smaller. His feet stopped wanting to stomp.

"Red swing is free!" the girl called. Asher felt excited. He ran fast. Dad pushed him high. "I see the whole park!" Asher said. He looked up at the sky. The clouds made a big white circle. He pumped his legs harder.

Then the swing went too high. Asher felt scared. "Stop, Daddy!" he yelled. Dad caught the swing. Asher climbed down slow. He sat in the sand and took one slow breath. Then he smiled. "Can we build a castle?" he asked. Dad sat down too. "Yes, let's build it big," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Adam wanted to write a note for Grandpa before bed. He got his crayons and some paper. He wrote all his letters in one long line. "ILOVEYOUGRANDPA," the paper said.

Grandpa came to say goodnight. He held the paper close. He turned it upside down. Then he turned it back. "Hmm," said Grandpa. "The letters are all squished together like a big storm of letters."

Adam looked at his paper. "Can you read my note?" he asked. Grandpa shook his head slowly. "Not yet, little one."

Then Adam saw his bedtime book on the pillow. He opened the front cover. The words had little gaps in them. One word, then a small space, then another word. Adam put his finger on the gap. "There is a space here," he said.

Adam took his crayon again. He drew small spaces in his note. Now it said, "I LOVE YOU GRANDPA." Grandpa read it out loud in a big, warm voice. He gave Adam a hug.

"Stinky feet need washing too," said Grandpa, and he laughed. Adam laughed too. Grandpa tucked him in and read the book from the front to the back. Adam's eyes got sleepy. "Don't forget my note," Adam whispered. Grandpa put it right by the lamp, where he could see it.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
The bookmobile came to Ethan's street. It was a big blue bus full of books. Ethan held his mama's hand. He wanted a library card of his very own.

Inside, the shelves were tall. The books were way up high. Ethan could not see the covers. "Too high," he said. He stretched his toes. Still too high.

Then he saw something in the back. A little corner with tiny shelves. The books there had big, bright covers. One was about a squishy frog. Ethan could reach it all by himself. "Mama, small books! For me!"

The library lady smiled. "That is the children's area," she said. "Books just for young kids like you." She helped Ethan write his name. His new card was blue, just like the bus.

Ethan picked the frog book. "Can I take him home for lunch?" he asked. The lady laughed. "He can sit next to your sandwich." Ethan carried the book to the desk. The lady beeped it with her scanner. Beep!

Ethan waved to the bookmobile as it drove away. He hugged the frog book tight. "See you, froggy," he whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Maya ran to the park with her bear, Bobo. She wanted to play house, but she had no house here. She looked around fast. She saw a big flat rock. She put Bobo on the rock. "This is your bed," she said.

Then she found a stick. She tapped the stick on the rock. "Time to eat, Bobo!" There was no food, really. But Maya made a face like she was stirring a pot. She held out her hand. "Here is your soup." Bobo said nothing. Maya pretended he ate it all up. She clapped. "You love soup!"

A boy named Sam ran over. He was holding his toy plane. "I am a pilot!" he said. He made a big zoom sound. Maya wanted to be on the plane too. But where could she sit? She looked at the ground.

She pointed at the wood chips. "This is the plane!" she said. She sat down and buckled an invisible belt. Sam sat next to her. He held his plane up high. "We fly to the beach!" Zoom, zoom! Maya heard the wind in the trees. It sounded just like a plane.

Then a dog ran by and grabbed Bobo! Maya jumped up. "My baby!" she cried. The dog dropped Bobo in the soft grass. Maya ran and picked him up. She hugged him tight. "We are home now, Bobo," she said. Sam zoomed his plane one more time over her head. "Good night, plane!" Maya called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Isiah sat at the little table in the school library. Miss Rosa put down a card with a big black B on it. "What sound does this make?" she asked.

"B," said Isaiah. Then he frowned. He wanted to write his own name, but he did not know how to start it.

Miss Rosa gave him a red crayon. Isaiah wrote i-s-a-i-a-h with a small i first. It looked wrong. His name did not look like his name.

Then Miss Rosa held up his name card. The first letter was a big I. It was tall and it seemed to shine on the paper.

Isiah rubbed out his small i. He drew a big I instead. "Isaiah!" he read out loud.

Miss Rosa clapped. Isaiah smiled and drew a ball next to his name, just for fun.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Bennett was at Grandma's house. Grandma was knitting a small blue blanket. "The baby is coming soon," she said. Bennett patted the tiny blanket. "Babies are so small," he said.

The next day, Dad took Bennett to the baby store. They pushed a big cart. Dad put in diapers. Then more diapers. Then even more diapers. Bennett counted them. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" A girl next to them stared. "Why so many diapers?" she asked her mom. Bennett listened hard.

At home, the baby came. Her name was Rosie. Rosie drank milk. Then Rosie made a wet diaper. Grandma changed it. Then Rosie drank more milk. Then another wet diaper. Grandma changed that one too. "Six diapers, then more," said Bennett. He put the diapers, one by one, into the basket.

Bennett picked up his pencil. He made a card for Rosie. Grandma helped him cut around the edges. One snip, then another snip. Rosie began to cry. She sounded sad. Bennett waited by her basket. Dad picked her up and rocked her. Soon Rosie went to sleep. Bennett laid the card beside her. "One baby, one card," he whispered. "Night night, Rosie."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Emmett sat at the dinner table. He wanted grapes. "Can I have three grapes?" he asked. Mom said, "Yes, three grapes for you."

Mom put grapes on his plate. One, two, three. But these grapes were big, big, big. Emmett looked at them. Were big grapes still three? Maybe big grapes counted as more?

He counted them with his finger. "One, two, three," he said. He pushed them apart. Still three. He pushed them together. Still three! He giggled. Big or small, three was three.

Then Dad slid over a bowl. "Look what I have." Dad counted his grapes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten little grapes!

Emmett leaned close. "Dad, do ten little grapes equal three big ones?" Dad laughed. "Count and see." Emmett pointed at his plate. "One, two, three." He pointed at the bowl. "Ten is more. Ten wins!"

Then Mom held up a rainbow cup. "Want three milk pours in here?" Emmett nodded. He watched the milk pour. "One, two, three," he said. He picked up a big grape and plopped it in. "Now it's a grape bath!"

Dad said, "You teach me something new every day." Emmett took a bite. "Three bites!" he said. "One, two, three."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: James wanted to build a tower of ten blocks. He patted the carpet flat first. He put down one block, then two blocks. Then he stopped. "What comes after two?" he asked himself. He could not think of it. His big sister was singing on the rug. She sang, "One, two, buckle my shoe." James listened. Three! He clapped his hands. The song gave him the word. He stacked three, then four, then five. The tower wobbled. It fell down with a big crash. James giggled and started again. His sister sat close and sang with him. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" James put on the last block, quick, before it could tip. The tower stood tall. "Ten blocks!" said James. His sister patted his head. Then James counted them all again, touching each one. "One, two, three," he sang, all the way up to ten.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Aurora waited at the gate for her daddy. The sun was warm on her nose. Her tummy rumbled. She wanted her snack right now. But first, her teacher said, everyone must wash hands. Aurora felt worried. "I am too hungry to wait," she said. Her teacher smiled. "Washing is quick," she said. "Then we eat."

Aurora stood at the little sink. She pumped one drop of soap onto her palm. She rubbed her hands under the water. Bubbles grew! She rubbed more, and the bubbles got thick and white. She spread them on her chin. Now she had a fluffy soap beard! Milo stood next to her, looking sad. He had dropped his cracker at snack time. Then he saw Aurora's white beard. He giggled and giggled.

Milo pumped soap too. He rubbed his hands with water. Bubbles grew on his hands too. He made soap whiskers. "We are bubble bears!" he said. The teacher laughed. Then they rinsed all the bubbles off. The teacher helped them dry their hands on the soft towel.

Daddy was at the gate now. He lifted Aurora up for a hug. "Tonight we will have your bath after dinner," he said. "Can I bring my rubber duck?" Aurora asked. Daddy kissed her soapy-smelling hair. "The duck, the boat, and both of us," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Carter went to the store with Mom. He wanted to find the squishy red ball. "Stay with me," said Mom. Carter held her hand.

Then he saw the balls far away. He let go of Mom's hand. He skipped down the big aisle. He turned around. He could not see Mom. The aisle was too long. Carter looked and looked. He walked back the way he came. Then he saw Mom's blue coat. He ran to her fast.

"There you are," said Mom. "I like to see you." Carter held her hand again. They found the red ball together. It was soft and squishy in his hands. At the checkout, a man pushed a cart of hot soup. "Step back," said Mom. Carter stepped back and waited. He squeezed his new ball and smiled. "Home now," he said. Mom squeezed his hand. They walked out the door together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Josephine sat at the art table. She picked up a red crayon. She drew a big red apple. Next to her, Ben drew a yellow sun. It looked warm and bright.

Josephine wanted to draw snow. She took white paper. She drew and drew. But her snow did not show up. The paper was white too. Her snow was hiding! She frowned. "I can't see my snow," she said.

Then she saw green paper in the bin. No, wait. She found blue paper. She drew soft white snow on it. Now the snow showed up! It was white on the blue. "Look, Ben!" she said. Ben smiled back. She drew a green tree under the snow. "I can share my blue paper," Josephine said. Ben gave her a hug. "That is not mean at all," he said. "That is nice." Josephine hung her picture up to dry.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Nova put on her clean dress. It was Eid morning. The street outside had flags and balloons. Music played, and it smelled like sweet bread.

Mama knelt down by the door. "When people come, you can say Eid Mubarak," she said. Nova practiced in a small voice. "Eid Mubarak." She tried again, a bit louder. Then the bell rang.

Nova opened the door. Auntie Ruby stood there with a sparkly bag. Nova took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak!" she said. Auntie Ruby smiled wide and hugged her. "Eid Mubarak to you too!" Then Uncle Ben came, and Nova said it again. Then Grandma came, and Nova said it once more.

Every time she said it, someone smiled at her. Then came a small surprise. A tiny cousin said it back to Nova, all by himself. Nova gave him a high five. "Eid Mubarak," she said, one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint green grass. But the green paint pot was empty. "Oh no," said Mia. She was painting grass too. Mia looked grumpy.

Then Mia dipped her brush in blue paint. She dipped it in yellow paint too. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned green! Hayden leaned close. He saw the blue and yellow make green.

"One dip blue, one dip yellow," Hayden said. He stirred his own brush round and round. Green! He painted tall grass. Mia painted a bunny in the grass. The sun did shine in the window. Their teacher smiled at the wet green paintings. "Bunny!" said Mia. "Grass!" said Hayden. They hung the pictures on the wall to dry.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen with her grandma. Grandma had warm toast on a big plate. "You can help," said Grandma. "Let's put butter on the toast."

Paisley picked up a little knife. Grandma held the knife too, so it stayed safe. Together they spread the butter. The butter went on soft and smooth. "Now watch," said Grandma.

Paisley looked at the toast. The butter was hard and yellow. Then it began to shine. Then it turned into a little wet puddle. Paisley touched the plate near the edge. "It's gone!" she said. "The butter ran away!"

Grandma smiled. "It melts on the warm toast," she said. "Look, it is still there. It is just soft now." Paisley leaned close. The butter had made the toast shiny all over. She took a small bite. The toast tasted good.

Next, Grandma gave Paisley a small cup. "Now we pour milk," she said. Paisley held the cup with both hands. Grandma held the little jug. They poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" said Paisley. Grandma clapped. Outside the window, a bird sat in a tree. Paisley waved at it with her milky cup.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara ran to school. Today was scarf day! She could not wait.

"Look at my scarf," said Ben. His scarf was long. It went down to his shoes. Clara held up her scarf. It was short. It stopped at her tummy.

"I want a long scarf," said Clara. "Mine is too short for the cold wind." She tried to stretch it. It would not grow. She frowned.

Then Clara had a big idea. "Let's share!" She put her short scarf on her neck. Ben wrapped his long scarf around her too. Now Clara was warm from top to toes.

At art time, Clara wanted to draw an ocean. The ocean was so big! Her paper was so small. "I will draw a short wave," she said. She drew a little wave and a big wave. It looked like the sea!

At nap time, Clara was sleepy. She snuggled into Ben's long scarf like a blanket. "Warm," she whispered. "Nice and warm."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Violet put on her new swim suit. Mom drove her to the pool by the lake. The water looked big and shiny in the light.

Violet stood at the edge. She wanted to swim. But she did not want to put her face in the water. "What if the water bites my nose?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. "Watch me," said Miss Kim. She leaned down. She put her mouth near the water. Then she blew. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles popped up.

Violet laughed at the bubbles. She leaned down too. She put her mouth close to the water. She blew. Bloop, bloop! The water did not bite at all. It made bubbles. Violet blew again, bigger this time. Mom clapped from her chair. Miss Kim held Violet's hand. "Again," said Violet, and she leaned down for more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Amelia wanted the little toy mouse. It lived in the big red box. The box sat on the small rug.

Tom put blocks in the box. Plunk, plunk. Then Sam took blocks out. Plunk, plunk. The mouse hid under the blocks each time.

"How will I find my mouse?" Amelia asked.

"Look in the box," said Miss Kim.

Amelia looked in. She saw blue blocks. She did not see the mouse. "Was that fast or slow?" Tom asked, dropping one block.

"Fast!" said Amelia. She laughed. Then Sam pulled blocks out, slow, one by one.

Miss Kim brought warm soup for snack. "Careful, it is hot," she said. She blew on Amelia's bowl. Amelia touched her cold cup of milk. Hot soup, cold milk.

The box got empty. All the blocks were out. Amelia peeked in again. There was the mouse! Its gray ears poked up.

"Hello, mouse," she said. "Do you want to grow bigger?" The mouse stayed small, of course.

Amelia put the mouse in her pocket. Then she put all the blocks back in the box. In, in, in. The rug looked tidy at last.

Sam held up one red block and smiled. "Out again?" he asked.

"No, Sam," said Amelia. "In!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Weston was hungry. The festival smelled like warm bread. His tummy made a big growl. "Was that a cloud rumbling?" asked Auntie May. Weston laughed. "That was me!"

They sat down at a long table. Many families sat there too. Weston saw big plates of rice and beans. He saw salty crackers in a bowl. He grabbed one cracker right away.

Then he saw that no one else was eating. Grandpa stood up. Grandpa said the family blessing. His voice was low and kind. Weston looked at his hand. He put the cracker down on his plate. He folded his hands and waited.

Grandpa said the last word. Then everyone picked up food at once. Weston munched his cracker. "It tastes better when we wait together," said Auntie May. Weston's tummy growled again. "There goes your thunder cloud," said Grandpa. Weston giggled so hard that a bean rolled off his plate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The wind blew hard outside. Sienna stood by the window with Mama. The big tree bent and swayed. Then all the lights went out. The room went dark.

Sienna grabbed Mama's hand. "The dark came," she said. "The wind did it," said Mama. "It knocked out the power." They heard the wind howl again. Sienna listened hard. Papa came with a flashlight. He clicked it on. The light came back, small and bright.

They sat on the couch together. Sienna held her plastic bunny. She looked out at the wind, then at the dark lamp. "Wind blows, lights sleep," she said. Mama smiled and wrapped her in a soft blanket. The rain tapped on the glass. The flashlight glowed warm. Soon the wind grew quiet. All the lights popped back on. Sienna waved at her bright lamp. "Hello, light," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Lincoln was at Grandma's house. His new baby sister was coming. Lincoln wanted to hold her, but he had to wait.

Grandma baked bread. Lincoln could smell it. The bread was warm and squishy. "Can baby sister eat bread?" he asked. "No," said Grandma. "Babies drink milk. Grown-ups feed her many times, day and night."

At night, Lincoln heard a small cry. Baby sister was awake. Mama fed her milk. In the morning, she cried again. Mama fed her again. "Baby eats one, two, three times, and more," said Lincoln. "Just like Grandma said."

Then Mama sat on the big soft couch. She put baby sister in Lincoln's arms. He held her very still. The baby made a tiny sound. Lincoln smiled and counted her little fingers, one, two, three, four, five.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Nicholas sat on his bed with his big bear book. He wanted Dad to read it. "Dad! Come read to me!" Dad came in and sat down.

Dad opened the book. He looked at the front page. Then he turned the pages one by one. He read from the front to the back. Nicholas watched Dad's eyes. They went along the little black marks. "Dad, what are those marks?" he asked. "Those are words," said Dad. "They tell me what to say."

Nicholas turned a page. This page had no marks on it. Only a big picture of a bear. "Read this one!" he said. Dad looked at the page. "There are no words here," he said. "Nothing is written on this page." Nicholas tapped the picture. "So the bear says nothing?" he asked. "The bear just looks," said Dad.

Nicholas turned to the next page. Little marks were there again. Dad read them out loud. The bear found honey! Nicholas clapped his hands. Then he turned back to the picture page. He made up his own words. "The bear is quiet," said Nicholas. Dad laughed. "That page is wrong," said Nicholas. "It has no words to read!" He turned the page and pointed. "Read this one, Dad. This one has words."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Eloise sat on her bedroom floor. Her teddy bear, Blue, sat on the table. Eloise wanted to hug him. But Blue was too far away.

Then Eloise saw her big brother Tom in the doorway. Tom had a big frown. His mouth turned down at the corners. His eyebrows made little hills.

"Tom looks sad," Eloise said. She felt sad too. She did not want Tom to be sad.

Eloise pointed to Tom's face. "You look sad," she said.

Tom nodded. "I lost my toy truck," he said.

Eloise looked under the table. She looked by the bed. Then she saw something red under the blanket. "Look!" she said.

Tom's frown went away. Now his mouth curved up. He was happy! He hugged the red truck. Then he hugged Eloise too.

Eloise smiled big. She felt excited and warm inside. Tom put Blue in her lap.

Eloise hugged her bear tight. "Happy faces," she said. Tom laughed and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Harrison went to the library with his mom. There was a big rug with pictures on it. Some pictures were animals. Some pictures were toys. Some pictures were foods.

A librarian gave Harrison a carrot, a plastic apple, and a plastic slice of bread. "Where do they go?" she asked. Harrison put the carrot with the toys. He put it next to the teddy bear. The librarian smiled and waited. Harrison looked and looked. Then he moved the carrot. He put it with the apple. He put it with the bread. "Apple, bread, carrot," he said. "Foods!" The librarian clapped.

Harrison picked up a black toy car. "Is this a food?" he asked. He answered himself. "No. It is a toy." He put the car with the toys. Then he sat down and made a vroom sound. His mom sat beside him and read him a book.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Anna climbed the big school bus. She held her lunchbox tight. It was red with a plane on it.

A boy sat down next to her. He had a red lunchbox too. It had a plane on it too!

"Oh no," said Anna. "Same lunchbox!"

The bus went bump, bump, bump. The two lunchboxes slid under the seat. Anna reached down. She picked one up. But which one was hers?

Then Anna looked at the lid. She saw letters there. "A-N-N-A," she read. "That is me! This one is mine!"

The boy looked at his lid too. "Tom," he said. "This one says Tom. That is me!"

Anna laughed. "Your name found your lunchbox," she said.

"My name is smart," said Tom. He grinned.

At school, the teacher helped them paint. Anna painted a big red plane. Under it, she painted her name.

"That is a smart picture," said Tom.

Anna held it up high. "Now everyone knows it is mine!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Myles wanted the puppy book. It was up on his bed. He climbed up next to it, not on the shelf, and held the book in his lap.

The book was upside down. The dog in the picture looked funny. Myles turned the book over. Now the dog sat right side up. "Good dog," said Myles.

He put his finger on the words. He started at the right side of the page. He slid his finger along. The words went the wrong way. Dad sat down next to him. Dad took Myles's hand. He set the finger down at the left side of the page. "Try here," said Dad.

Myles slid his finger from left to right. The words marched along in a line, one after another. Dad read them out loud. "The puppy chewed his fresh bone all day." Myles laughed. The puppy had chewed a big hole!

Myles turned to the front page. He turned pages one by one, front to back. Each page had more words. Each page had more puppy. He slid his finger from left to right again and again.

At the last page, the puppy was asleep. "The end," said Dad. Myles hugged the book. "Read it again!" said Myles. Dad smiled and turned back to the front.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Luca stood at the bus stop with Mama. The sun came out. "Sunny now," said Luca. But the wind blew hard. His hat flew off. "Wind," said Luca. Mama picked up his hat. She put it back on his head.

Yesterday it had rained. Luca saw water on the ground. A big puddle sat by the bench. "Look, Mama! Water!"

"Rain made that puddle," said Mama. Luca stepped in the puddle. Splash! His shoe got wet. He stepped again. Splash, splash!

"My boot is wet," said Luca. He frowned. "Cold foot."

"We can fix that," said Mama. She opened her big bag. She pulled out dry socks. "I was ready for puddles." Luca sat on the bench. He chewed his cracker while Mama put the dry socks on his feet. Warm again!

Then Luca looked up. Little white flakes fell down. "Snow!" said Luca. Mama zipped his coat up high. She put his mittens on his hands.

"Snow makes the ground white," said Luca. He pointed at the bench. The snow sat on top, soft and thin.

The bus came around the corner. Luca jumped up like a spring. He held Mama's hand tight. They climbed the big steps together.

"Bye, puddle!" Luca called out the window.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Sofia was going camping with her family. She packed her little bear in a bag. "Time to get in the car," said Mama. Sofia climbed into her car seat. She was so excited. She hugged her bear tight. But the straps hung loose. Nobody clicked the buckle.

Daddy sat in the front. He looked back. "Hmm," he said. "The car will not go yet." Sofia waited. The car was still. "Why is the car waiting?" she asked. She looked down at her seat. Then she heard it. Click! Daddy had buckled her straps snug and safe.

The car started to roll. "The car heard the click!" said Sofia. Outside, the trees went by. Sofia felt the soft strap on her chest. She held her bear on her lap. "Now we can pretend to drive far away," she said. "Beep beep," said Daddy, and they drove on.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Iris went to the pharmacy with Grandpa. The pharmacy sold soap, and Iris wanted the pink soap. "We need soap for hand washing," said Grandpa. Iris picked a pink bottle. "Good pick," said Grandpa. "You are so smart."

At home, Iris had to use the toilet. Then she ran to the sink. But the sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water. "I can't wash!" she cried.

Grandpa brought a step stool. He set it by the sink. He stood right next to her. Iris climbed up. Now her hands reached the water! She pumped the pink soap. Grandpa said, "Wash while we count to twenty." They counted together. One, two, three, all the way to twenty.

The bubbles went down the drain. Iris held her hands up to the sun by the window. They were shiny and clean. "Now I can eat my sandwich," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Henry sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow up a hill. The wind outside made a windy sound. Henry rolled down his window a little bit.

"My cup is empty," said Henry. He tipped it upside down. Not one drop came out. "I want it full," he said.

Dad stopped the car at a little shop. He bought cold water from the big fridge. Dad poured the water into Henry's cup. Henry watched. He poured too fast at first, and water splashed over the top. "Whoa," said Henry. Dad poured slow instead. The water went up and up. It stopped right at the top. The cup was full now, not empty.

Henry drank a little. The water was cold on a hot day. "We pay for the water here," said Dad, and Henry helped put the coins on the counter.

Back in the car, Henry held his full cup with two hands. He took one small sip. "Slow," said Henry. Dad smiled and drove slowly down the hill.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Daniel went to the park with Grandma. The sun was warm. The water in the little creek was cold. Daniel put one toe in. "Brrr," he said. He pulled his toe out fast. Cold water made him shiver.

Daniel saw something red by the bench. It was a little lighter. Grandma had one like it at home. Grandma used it for the big candle. Daniel did not touch it. He kept his hands in his pockets. He ran to Grandma. "I see something," he said. He pointed with one finger.

Grandma walked over slow. She looked down. She picked up the lighter. "Good boy," she said. "That is for grown-ups." She put it in her bag. Then they fed the ducks together. The ducks splashed in the water. Daniel laughed and clapped. Soon the sky turned orange. It was getting late. "Time to go," said Grandma. Daniel held her hand all the way home.
